reason: The chamber has a marked pumping-wall slot, and heart muscle fits that role.
expectation: The heart muscle will form the chambers' pumping walls.

effect: Heart muscle filled the pumping-wall slot; the chambers still need direction control.
reaction: The thickening walls make the pumping role clear.
reason: The valves match the remaining direction-control slot and their picture shows them preventing reverse flow.
expectation: The valves will fit into the chambers to control flow direction.

effect: The valves now control flow through the chambers; the pump still needs a rhythm.
reaction: The opposing arrows clearly show how the valves prevent reverse flow.
reason: The pacemaker cells produce a spreading electrical wave, which suggests they can give the fitted chambers a rhythm.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will give the pump a regular rhythm.

effect: The pacemaker completed the beating heart, leaving the returning route and blood to assemble.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites suggest it belongs inside the red-cell envelopes to make oxygen-carrying cells.
expectation: The hemoglobin will fill the envelopes to make red blood cells that carry oxygen.

effect: The red blood cells are ready to add to the blood; they make ATP from sugar despite lacking mitochondria.
reaction: It is interesting that these cells still make ATP without mitochondria.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The plasma and red blood cells formed oxygen-carrying blood; the heart and vessel route still need to be connected.
reaction: The picture makes the different places for hemoglobin and dissolved sugar clear.
reason: The capillary networks can connect the branching arteries and veins into a returning route.
expectation: The vessels and capillaries will form a connected circulation route.

effect: The capillaries linked the arteries and veins into a circuit with slots for a pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked connections make the route back to the pump clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted into the vessel circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is connected to the vessel circuit; the transport medium still needs to be added.
reaction: The outgoing and returning connections make the heart's place in the circuit clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the circuit's transport-medium slot.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit as its transport medium.

effect: The blood completed the circuit, showing how capillaries exchange materials with tissue while blood returns to the heart.
reaction: The exchange inset makes the connection between circulation and cellular supplies clearer.

mostWorthwhile.text: Completing the circuit was most worthwhile because it brought the pump, blood and vessels together and showed how the same route serves tissues.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding plasma to the red blood cells felt predictable, though it was a clear intermediate step.

surprise.text: I was surprised that red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria or nucleus.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the named slots and pictures gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the circulation connects with other body systems. The tissue-exchange picture suggests a useful next link, although most combinations in this chapter were straightforward.
